items.title: Fetching Document Files with React and RTK Query: A Practical Guide
items.author: Nour Mustafa
items.description:
In modern web applications, efficiently fetching and displaying various document files — such as images and PDFs — can be a challenge. This article details how to use React and RTK Query to streamline this process. We will use DummyJSON as our data source in a practical example of fetching an image.

Step 1: Setting Up Redux with RTK Query

First, we need to set up our Redux store and define an API slice using createApi from Redux Toolkit. This will allow us to manage our API calls.

// **imageApi.ts**
import { createApi, fetchBaseQuery } from "@reduxjs/toolkit/query/react";
// Define a service using a base URL and expected endpoints
export const imageApi = createApi({
  reducerPath: "dummyjsonApi",
  baseQuery: fetchBaseQuery({ baseUrl: "<https://dummyjson.com>" }),
  endpoints: (builder) => ({
    getImage: builder.query({
      query: () => ({
        url: "/image/150",
        responseHandler: async (response) =>
          URL.createObjectURL(await response.blob()),
        cache: "no-cache",
      }),
    }),
  }),
});
// Export hooks for usage in functional components
export const { useGetImageQuery } = imageApi;

In this setup:

  • We define an API slice called imageApi with a single endpoint, getImage, which fetches an image from DummyJSON.

Why Use responseHandler?

  1. Handling Binary Data:
  • By default, when you make a request for a resource, the response is usually handled as JSON. However, when dealing with images or other binary formats, we need to process the response differently.
  • The responseHandler allows us to define a custom way to handle the response, enabling us to treat it as a blob (binary large object) instead of JSON.

2. Creating Object URLs:

  • When we fetch an image, we receive a response containing binary data. The responseHandler is used to read this data as a blob and then create a URL that can be used as the source for an <img> tag or any other element that requires a URL.
  • The URL.createObjectURL() method converts the blob into a string URL that the browser can use to display the image.

Step 2: Configuring the Redux Store

Next, we configure the Redux store to include our API slice.

// **store.ts**
import { configureStore } from "@reduxjs/toolkit";
import { setupListeners } from "@reduxjs/toolkit/query";
import { imageApi } from "./api";

export const store = configureStore({
  reducer: {
    [imageApi.reducerPath]: imageApi.reducer,
  },
  middleware: (getDefaultMiddleware) =>
    getDefaultMiddleware().concat(imageApi.middleware),
});
// Setup listeners for refetching data on focus and reconnect
setupListeners(store.dispatch);

Here, we add the imageApi reducer to our store and set up middleware to enable caching and other RTK Query features.

Step 3: Rendering the Application

In our main application file, we set up the Redux Provider to make the store available throughout our component tree.

// **main.tsx**
import { StrictMode } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import App from "./App.tsx";
import "./index.css";
import { Provider } from "react-redux";
import { store } from "./redux/store";

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <Provider store={store}>
      <App />
    </Provider>
  </StrictMode>
);

Step 4: Fetching and Displaying the Image

Finally, we can implement our App component to use the useGetImageQuery hook, which retrieves the image and manages loading and error states.

//**App.tsx**
import { useGetImageQuery } from "./redux/api";
function App() {
  const { data: imageSrc, isLoading, isError } = useGetImageQuery({});
  const content = isLoading ? (
      <p className="text-lg font-bold text-blue-700">Loading...</p>;
    ) : isError ? (
      <p className="text-lg font-bold text-red-700">Error</p>;
    ) : (
      <img src={imageSrc} />;
    );
    return <div className="flex justify-center items-center my-32">{content}</div>;
  }
export default App;

In this component:

  • We call useGetImageQuery to fetch the image from DummyJSON.
  • Depending on the query state (isLoading, isError), we conditionally render a loading indicator, an error message, or the fetched image.

Summary

In summary, the responseHandler is essential for properly handling binary data when fetching images or other non-JSON resources. It allows us to transform the response into a format suitable for rendering in our application.

Full source code in the repo below: [GitHub repository](https://github.com/nour-aldin/Fetching-Document-Files-with-React-and-RTK-Query)

items.title: Implementing separate guards for different controllers in Nestjs
items.author: Nour Mustafa
items.description:
Guard is a common pattern to control program flow.
It makes conditional checks to determine the code execution should continue or exit.
Using guards improve readability and maintainability of your code.

Guards in NestJS lifecycle

The request lifecycle in NestJS refers to the sequence of events handling an incoming request and outgoing response.

As defined in the diagram below, an incoming request passes through several components including middleware, guards, interceptors, and pipes before arriving at the endpoint where a response is generated. Each component has a role in processing the request and its subsequent response. Guards are executed following any specified middleware and before interceptors.

Guards can be applied on three different levels:

  1. Global
  2. Controller
  3. Route

The sequence of execution starts with global guards → controller guards → route guards, as shown below.

By understanding this sequence, we can take advantage of various lifecycle events. For example, we can create a global guard to ensure that only users with a valid token can access the app, then creating role guard to configure the user controller to only allow the admin user to access it.

Ideally, global guards provide general protections across all modules, while controller and route guards give more specific access control.

Requirement

We want to create the following Auth, and ApiKey modules, where each module should use a different guard mechanism.

To achieve this, we will work on the Controller guards level as shown below.

Create AuthGuard

In the example below we create a simple guard that allows access to a route only if the request includes a valid Authorization header:

//auth.guard.ts
@Injectable()
export class AuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const request = context.switchToHttp().getRequest();

    // we use a hardcoded string to validate the req headers for simplicity
    const token = request.headers['authorization'];

    if (!token) throw new UnauthorizedException('Token is not available');

    if (token !== 'valid-token')
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Unauthorized Access Token');

    return true;
  }
}

The above example utilizes the switchToHttp. method to obtain an HttpArgumentsHost object suitable for the HTTP application context. Then the request object is extracted from the HttpArgumentsHost object, and the request headers are examined to confirm the presence of a valid token.

For this simple example, we use a hardcoded string to validate the user for the sake of simplicity. In a real-world application, it’s advisable to use information from a JWT token or to validate against a database.

Create ApiKeyGuard

In the example below we create a simple guard that allows access to a route only if the request includes a valid apiKey query:

//apiKey.guard.ts
@Injectable()
export class ApiKeyGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const request = context.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const { apiKey } = request.query;

    if (!apiKey) throw new UnauthorizedException('ApiKey is not available');

    // we use a hardcoded string to validate the req query for simplicity
    if (apiKey !== 'valid-api-key')
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid ApiKey');

    return true;
  }
}

The request object here is extracted from the HttpArgumentsHost object and the request query params are examined to confirm the presence of a valid apiKey.

To apply the implemented guards, we’ll use useGuards() decorator provided from NestJS and pass the required guard in as it’s parameter.

//auth.controller.ts
@Controller('auth')
@UseGuards(AuthGuard) // here we apply AuthGuard for Auth Controller
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private readonly authService: AuthService) {}

  @Get()
  getHello(): string {
    return 'Hello, from Auth controller!';
  }
}
//apiKey.controller.ts
@Controller('api-key')
@UseGuards(ApiKeyGuard) // here we apply ApiKeyGuard for ApiKey Controller
export class ApiKeyController {
  constructor(private readonly apiKeyService: ApiKeyService) {}

  @Get()
  getHello(): string {
    return 'Hello, from ApiKey controller!';
  }
}

Result

  1. Auth Module:

If we send a request with empty or an invalid authorization header as below, we’ll get a response with HTTP status code 403:

With a correct header, the request is successful:

2. apiKey Module:

If we send a request with empty or an invalid apiKey query param as below, we’ll get a response with HTTP status code 403:

With a correct query, the request is successful:
